proposals.trigger: Gap remains after contingency and the APS-specific lines are exhausted (owner has dropped to the weak tier, M-A), while the CIP widens its definition of capital investment to include maintenance that extends life by 5+ years.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds an extra funding source for the gap, available only to sites with an existing-asset component (C-type), not N-type that need new poles. It competes with the existing hardware-replacement priorities (e.g. the controller firewall replacements), so each site served this way may bring a different site delay. In effect it is a second route into the b_hw allowance of PW5, used reactively.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. PW5 gives APS add-on funding at hardware replacement through b_hw (U($0, $300k)), but only as a rule-driven event at rate lambda_hw, not as a reaction to an overrun. D3.5 F-k covers the director 10% / SG000 reserve. Re-labelling at the point of overrun is not modelled.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.2: FY27-31 CIP intends to widen the definition of capital investment to cover maintenance extending life 5+ years (CIPpol p.10); 2025-02 budget option 'restructure work orders so they count as capital' (T/staffing/sfmta-media-41700.txt p.9, p.17); signals are one of the most degraded assets and SGR funding is 'extremely limited' (CIPpol p.10). 01 s2.1: EP17 $1M went to the ~98 controllers with firewall flaws, though a 2023 PIF listed APS replacement as eligible (OCT25 p.7). Also 01 s2.1: 'riding together with existing work is cheapest'.
proposals.parameter: q_relabel and b_relabel
proposals.range: q_relabel U(0, 0.5) probability that a C-type overrun site can be recoded; b_relabel U($0, $400k) per year pooled with and capped by b_hw; zero for N-type sites. Sites funded this way enter the internal queue and are subject to K_crew.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-f gap source order (contingency, then relabel pool, then q_topup) and D3.3 PW5 (shares the b_hw account).

proposals.behaviour: Paper commitment (placeholder CIP line) in place of an application. Under pressure, the grant-preparation staff list an 'APS' line in the capital plan against a hoped-for grant source, and cite that line when pressed. No application follows, or one that cannot qualify. The line absorbs pressure. It is not money, and it is not counted as funded.
proposals.trigger: A pressure event (advocate meeting, disability council) when the task is IDLE or the window is closed or unpreparable, and the 'no money' reply alone would leave pressure high.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds a third branch to the pressure event, next to DEFLECTED and 'pressure stays'. With probability p_placate, pressure(t) is cut to (1 - psi) of its value, so later p_start is lowered. The affected intersections get a flag 'listed_unfunded' that makes no money flow and is not counted in the funded count. The model gains an output 'reported_covered minus funded' for the gap between what is announced and what is installed. A later window finds a paper line already 'occupying' the slot, with probability q_stale that it is never converted into an application.
proposals.already_in_model: Not found. 02 D3.1 has only two branches: DEFLECTED (pressure leaves no effect) and pressure remaining in pressure(t). D3.5 F-a to F-m has no 'listed but not applied' state.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.1 row 'Resources' (SG136 'APS FY25' has no funding row in the FY27-31 table); 01 §2.2 row 'Events' (FY25-29 CIP planned SG136 $1.0M from 'HSIP Cycle 12', yet none of the 330 C12 applications was an SF APS application); 01 §3.1 hard facts (SG142 $488,144 is pure APS and ineligible in C13 as written, and exceeds the $360k cap); 01 §2.1 row 'Decision rule' (share reported to MDC fell from 'most' in 2023 to about 1/3 in 2026). Quote: 'SG136 APS FY25 ... no funding row'. These are facts about plan lines, not proof of intent.
proposals.parameter: p_placate (probability) and psi (pressure reduction factor), plus q_stale (placeholder never converted)
proposals.range: p_placate U(0, 0.4), taken from the 1 - p_deflect share only; psi U(0.2, 0.8); q_stale U(0.3, 1.0). The switch sw_paper = 0 recovers the current model.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 pressure-event branch (adds a branch that reduces pressure(t)); D4 outputs (adds the reported-versus-funded gap)

proposals.behaviour: Risk-averse submission margin. Staff do not submit a package whose BCR is only just above the 5.0 gate. Failure costs more than the lost chance. A rejected or delayed project brings red flags, a 5-year clock, a PIF problem, and possibly returned pre-construction funds. So they submit only when BCR clears 5.0 by a safety margin, or they drop the lowest-BCR intersections until it does.
proposals.trigger: A computed package BCR in [5.0, 5.0 x (1 + margin)); more so when strain(t) is high, when the construction start date is close to the award date, or when a red flag is already on file.
proposals.effect_in_model: The packing stop rule and the submit gate change from 'whole-package BCR >= 5.0' to 'BCR >= 5.0 x (1 + margin)'. Marginal packages become F-a (not submitted), which cuts the number of instances and shifts the intersections to later windows or to the local track. The margin could also scale with the size of strain(t), so overload makes staff more cautious.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. The 5.0 gate (D3.3, F-a) and the kappa_cont contingency exist. No behavioural safety margin for delivery risk exists. Red flags only enter through rho_flag and F-d.
proposals.evidence: 01 §3.1 hard facts, 'schedule risk': SG142 construction is planned for 2027-07 but C13 approval is 2027-03/04, and the observed grant-to-construction time in past SF rounds is 15-28 months; federal money built in-house needs a PIF first. 01 §2.1 constraints: the two-year gap between approval and cycle start. 02 D3.5 F-d (red flags hurt later rounds). No direct statement of a margin policy: no document support for the margin itself.
proposals.parameter: bcr_margin
proposals.range: U(0, 0.5); the extra margin could also scale with strain(t) as bcr_margin x (1 + a x strain(t)). 0 reproduces the current gate.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.3 packing algorithm step 3 (stop rule) and step 4, and the pre-submission gate 'BCR >= 5.0'

proposals.behaviour: Labor-recovery bias in choosing what to package. Part of the signal electrician staff is paid from the project-support fund, expected to be recovered from capital projects, and operating deficits are large. A capital-application preparer therefore favours packages that put in-house Signal Shop hours onto grant-funded jobs (C-type, no excavation) over larger or outsourced packages, even when those would help more intersections.
proposals.trigger: The operating deficit and staffing pressure are high, and the shop has a vacancy it must cover from capital funds. Every packaging round triggers it.
proposals.effect_in_model: The sort key in packing step 2 changes from the pure BCR rank to BCR x (1 + w_labor x in_house_flag). C-type intersections that can be built in-house enter first, and N-type packages (outsourced or on a corridor) are crowded out or delayed. A package also counts as a funding win for a different reason, so the choice of which intersections receive money shifts without any change in the money available.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. K_crew and strain(t) limit supply of work (D3.2, D3.4). The incentive to pick work that pays for labor is not a rule. The packing order is pure BCR.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.1 row 'Resources': 8 of 21 electrician positions sit on the project-support fund, 'expected to be recovered by capital projects' (ASO27 p.123), labelled fact with the meaning marked inference. 01 §2.1 row 'Incentive': grants that pay Signal Shop labor can ease the operating deficit, so SFMTA has a motive to seek APS grants (CIPpol p.10, marked inference). 01 §2.2 row 'Decision rule': 2025-02 budget options, 'restructure work orders so they count as capital' (sfmta-media-41700 p.9, p.17; Signal Shop not named).
proposals.parameter: w_labor
proposals.range: U(0, 1.0); the in_house_flag is the carrier type C with internal construction. 0 reproduces the current BCR-only order.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.3 packing algorithm step 2 (candidate sort order)

proposals.behaviour: Request-list triage that shrinks the denominator. Instead of funding more, staff reclassify requests: close them as 'covered by an engineering project', 'already compliant', or 'infeasible', or merge near-duplicates. The count that the council hears falls, and the story 'most are being handled' can be told without more installs.
proposals.trigger: A council meeting or report where the unfunded share has to be stated; stronger when the parent-project status of many requests is uncertain.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds a list-hygiene event: each month, with rate lambda_prune, a pending intersection moves from the backlog to a 'closed_admin' state. It leaves the denominator of the reported coverage share, but it is still in never_served and in the crash-based need data. This separates 'reported unfunded share' from 'real never_served set', which the model uses to compare mechanisms. The prune choice favours the highest-cost and lowest-scored intersections.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. D3.1 says an intersection returns to the pool only after all instances end. Records of the 3 completed parent projects (done3, 'recorded late' scenario) and pi (parent project still in scope) exist, but they are data uncertainty, not a behaviour by staff. There is no actor-driven closure.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.1 row 'Decision rule': reported counts change across years (2018: 20 of 71 under way; 2023: 'most will be installed in recent years', about 70; 2026: about 75 with 'about one third' covered by projects, the rest 'selected based on funding'). 01 §3.2 (the 3 parents marked complete, 'done3', list may lag). No document shows staff closing requests on purpose: no document support for the behaviour; the evidence is only that the count and framing moved.
proposals.parameter: lambda_prune and prune_rank (which intersections go first)
proposals.range: lambda_prune U(0, 0.1) per year per pending intersection (0 reproduces the current model); prune_rank in {highest cost first, lowest score first, random}
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 intersection occupancy / pool release; D4 outputs (adds 'reported share' next to never_served)

proposals.behaviour: Descope and re-sequence the batch (value engineering). Keep the no-dig sites, strip or defer the sites that need new conduit or curb ramps, and spend the freed money on more cheap sites. The staff member decides at the design-complete node, before asking anyone for money.
proposals.trigger: Design-complete node (t_des) shows the batch cost above planned cost x (1+kappa_cont). The staff member first compares the gap with the cost of dropping the worst sites.
proposals.effect_in_model: Replaces 'ask for top-up, else TERMINATE the site' with a third option. Dig-heavy sites go to a DEFERRED_DIG sub-pool. The remaining sites are installed within the existing money, so more sites are served early and the dig sites wait. This changes the order in which sites are served, and the share of sites that end as never_served.
proposals.already_in_model: Not captured. F-f (02 section D3.5) only has contingency, then q_topup, then TERMINATED, and the whole path is decided by Z draws. D3.4 'termination' returns a site to the pool but does not let staff choose which sites to drop. Packing (D3.3) selects by BCR, not by dig-or-no-dig. No existing rule is a staff choice among sites after design.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.2: SG142 is written as 'about 22 intersections, no excavation, all built by Signal Shop' (CIP27m l.292-294, l.2511). That shows SFMTA already frames the cheap no-dig subset as a separate deliverable. No document shows staff dropping sites after an overrun, so that step is inference.
proposals.parameter: p_descope
proposals.range: 0 to 1 (default sensitivity 0, 0.5, 0.9). Also d_floor = minimum share of batch sites that must stay (0.5 to 1).
proposals.rule_modified: F-f gap handling in D3.5 and the D3.4 queue entry rule. When the gap exceeds the contingency, with probability p_descope the highest-cost sites are moved to the pool until the gap is closed, instead of drawing q_topup.

proposals.behaviour: Shift the curb-ramp part of the overrun to the Public Works curb ramp program. The staff member splits the cost so SFMTA keeps conduit and APS hardware, and asks Public Works to build the ramps from its own ramp budget. The staff member argues that the ramps are Public Works scope anyway.
proposals.trigger: Gap is mostly ramp cost (ramp share of overrun above a threshold) and a ramp contract or ramp budget line exists in the same fiscal year.
proposals.effect_in_model: Cuts the SFMTA-side gap by shift_share x ramp cost. Adds a delay t_ramp_wait to the site, because the site waits for the Public Works ramp schedule. Moves cost from cost_by_actor of SFMTA to Public Works. The delay may push the site past a window or milestone and trigger F-d or F-g style slippage.
proposals.already_in_model: Not captured. D3.4 has 'merge into existing project' (a parent project in the sense of PW4), which moves a site into another project's scope. It has no partial split of one cost item to another agency, and F-f funds a gap only from contingency or q_topup. D3.5 F-g covers a partner project's delay but not a deliberate hand-off of cost.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.11: Public Works designs ramps and reserves for future APS, but 'ramp construction does not trigger APS; APS is MTA's job' (MDC26t). Ramp budget FY26 $4.0M, requested $8.1M and $12.2M for FY27/28. Contract 35 ramp delay is about 8 years (OCT25 p.27). The same lines show the shift would be slow, and that Public Works resists taking APS scope.
proposals.parameter: shift_ramp
proposals.range: Share of ramp cost moved: 0 to 0.7. Acceptance probability q_dpw: 0.2 to 0.8 (inferred). Added delay t_ramp_wait: 6 to 36 months, from the Contract 35 and 36 durations.
proposals.rule_modified: F-f in D3.5: the gap is reduced by shift_ramp x ramp cost before q_topup is drawn. The shifted ramp work starts a delay timer on the site in D3.4.

proposals.behaviour: Park the designed site instead of terminating it, and use the finished design as a readiness argument in the next funding cycle. The staff member keeps the design shelf-ready, waits for the next 5YPP or CIP window, and files again with a higher readiness score.
proposals.trigger: The gap is not covered by contingency and q_topup is refused (or not attempted), while the design is complete and still valid.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds a HELD state between 'no top-up' and TERMINATED. The site keeps its design and does not return to the pool as a new site. After hold months it re-enters the funding queue with a bonus on the application success rate. Reduces repeat design cost and raises the chance of success in the next window, but uses up a design shelf-life (design may go stale).
proposals.already_in_model: Partly different. D3.4 'project termination' cancels all remaining events and sends the site back to the pool as a plain site, with no memory of design. F-f says an unfunded gap means TERMINATED. F-j mentions 'wait for the next 5YPP' for Prop L amendments, but only for the policy path, not for a designed site. No rule gives a design-complete site better chances.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3: Prop L 5YPP scoring gives readiness the maximum 5 points out of 31 (EP17-5YPP p.12-13). Section 2.2: the CIP rule is to fund 'urgent needs in phases (raising project or grant readiness)' (CIPpol p.6). The idea that a finished design wins a later bid is inference from these scoring lines.
proposals.parameter: t_hold and b_ready
proposals.range: t_hold (months in HELD before re-entering): 6 to 30. b_ready (additive boost to approval probability at re-entry): 0 to 0.2. d_stale = design validity limit, 36 to 84 months; beyond this the design is redone and costs a share of the original design cost.
proposals.rule_modified: F-f and the D3.4 termination clause: 'no top-up' goes to HELD (not TERMINATED) with probability p_hold; HELD sites re-enter the next local or HSIP window with the b_ready boost.

proposals.behaviour: Reclassify part of the overrun as state-of-good-repair work on existing signal assets. The staff member argues that new conduit and pole work is replacement of failing infrastructure, so it can be charged to the signals and SGR line, not to the APS line.
proposals.trigger: The gap is mostly conduit or other work that also repairs existing equipment, and the CIP definition of capital investment is being widened.
proposals.effect_in_model: Part of the gap is covered by a source outside the APS-specific lines, with no top-up request to SFCTA. The cost is taken from other signal projects, so the model should show an opportunity cost (a later SGR delay) and not new money. It raises the covered share of the gap and lowers the load on q_topup.
proposals.already_in_model: Not captured. F-k covers the director's 10 percent and the SG000 reserve as a start-up source, with 'no spare margin' as the failure. F-f only offers contingency or q_topup. No rule lets staff relabel the cost type. Excluded as duplicate if the author reads F-k as covering the SG000 reserve for gap filling; flagged here because F-k does not say that.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.2: signals are 'one of the most degraded SFMTA assets', SGR money is 'extremely limited' (CIPpol p.10). The FY27-31 CIP proposes to widen the capital investment definition to cover maintenance that extends life by 5 or more years (CIPpol p.10). The 2025 budget options include 'reorganize work orders to count as capital projects' (sfmta-media-41700 p.9, p.17), not specific to Signal Shop. Whether staff do this for APS has no document support.
proposals.parameter: q_reclass and f_reclass
proposals.range: q_reclass (probability the reclass is allowed): 0.1 to 0.6 (inferred). f_reclass (share of the gap covered if allowed): 0.1 to 0.5. Optional side cost: delay of other SGR signal work, 3 to 12 months.
proposals.rule_modified: F-f in D3.5: after contingency and before q_topup, draw q_reclass; if allowed, reduce the gap by f_reclass x gap.

proposals.behaviour: Site swap / backfill instead of terminate. When design shows that some sites need new conduit and curb ramps and the total exceeds contingency, the funding preparer removes the expensive sites from the funded batch and substitutes cheaper pool sites (existing conduit and pole usable, no dig). Alternatively the expensive sites are deferred to a later phase while the cheap ones go ahead. The batch money is kept and a top-up request is avoided. The cost is that the hard sites are served last or never, so the pool drifts toward costly sites.
proposals.trigger: At the design-complete node (the F-f discovery point), when the site-level overrun would use up the batch contingency kappa_cont and the batch gap would need a top-up request.
proposals.effect_in_model: Changes the F-f branch for a gap beyond contingency. Today the options are only top-up (q_topup) or TERMINATED with the site back to the pool. New branch: with probability p_swap, expensive sites are returned to the pool and the freed money pays for the cheapest unserved C-type sites from the pool. The substitute sites need a fresh design delay t_des and their own overrun draw, and installs resume only after that. The pool's mean unit cost rises (feeds costpress), the number of sites served per dollar rises, and the sites that are never served become systematically the costly ones.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. F-f already terminates the project or site and returns it to the pool. D3.1 already lets the pool release sites for repacking. But nothing back-fills the batch with cheaper sites while keeping the money, and no policy chooses which sites to drop. Not fully captured, so kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.2 and the CIP row: SG142 is written as 'about 22 sites, no excavation, all built by Signal Shop' (CIP27m l.292-294, l.2511), which shows the planners already sort by dig versus no-dig. 01 s3.2 (SG017 scope) says new APS is allowed 'where existing conduits and poles are in satisfactory condition'. No document shows a swap after design.
proposals.parameter: p_swap
proposals.range: U(0, 0.8) as the probability of choosing swap over top-up request at the discovery node. Add a second switch sw_defer in {terminate, swap, defer_to_phase2}. If defer, the site waits t_defer = U(6, 24) months in a Phase-2 queue and then re-enters PREPARING.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-f recovery branch, plus the D3.4 local-batch site selection rule (add a cost-ascending back-fill step).

proposals.behaviour: Cost carve-out by reattribution. The preparer argues that the new conduit and curb ramps are not APS costs. The ramp part is assigned to the Public Works curb-ramp program, and the conduit part to signal state-of-good-repair or a corridor or signal-upgrade partner project. The APS application then carries only the hardware cost. The overrun on the APS line shrinks. The price is dependence on someone else's schedule.
proposals.trigger: Design finds that conduit and ramp work adds more cost than contingency covers, and a Public Works ramp contract or a partner signal project exists at or near the site.
proposals.effect_in_model: A fraction phi_carve of the conduit and ramp cost (the c_full add-ons q_pipe and q_ramp, about $200k each) is moved off the batch ledger, so the funding gap falls and fewer top-up requests are needed. The site becomes dependent on a partner: it gets the t_partner delay and the q_partner_cancel risk of F-g, with ramp work following the Public Works contract timeline (the ledger cites 6-9.5 years for Contracts 35/36). The recorded cost per actor shifts to Public Works. Installs happen later but cost less per site on the APS line.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. D3.4 and F-g handle sites that ride a parent project (Fs path, t_parent, t_partner), but the assignment is made once, when the site enters the list. The dynamic move of costs to a partner at the moment of overrun is not written down. F-f states 'the same cost is counted once', which blocks a re-split rather than modelling it. Kept as a distinct switch.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.11: 'Ramps are designed for future APS, but ramp construction does not trigger APS; APS is the MTA's job' (MDC26t); ramp budget sits in a separate Public Works line (FY26 $4.0M, FY27/28 $8.1M/$12.2M). 01 s2.2: the FY27-31 CIP proposes to 'broaden the definition of capital investment' and a budget option reads 'restructure work orders so they count toward capital projects'. No document shows an APS-specific carve-out, so that part has no document support.
proposals.parameter: phi_carve
proposals.range: U(0, 0.7) as the share of conduit and ramp cost reassigned, applied only to sites with a live partner project (probability q_partner_avail U(0.1, 0.5)). Reassigned sites inherit t_partner and q_partner_cancel.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-f (gap computation), linked to F-g and the D3.4 Fs and merged-into-project delivery rules.

proposals.behaviour: Top-up request timed to a funding window and chosen by channel. The preparer does not file the request at the discovery moment. It is held for the next budget cycle, a 5YPP amendment, a quarterly allocation request, or the Director's 10% adjustment authority, whichever opens first and has the best fit. Each channel has its own approval chance and wait. During the wait the site is held at the design-complete stage.
proposals.trigger: A funding gap beyond contingency has been found, and no channel is open immediately.
proposals.effect_in_model: Replaces the single q_topup draw (with t_pause only in F-e) by a two-part draw: a wait time until the earliest usable window, and a channel-specific approval probability. Installs of the affected sites slip by the wait. Channels with shorter waits (director adjustment, unassigned signal reserve) have smaller capacity, so they run out. The result is a time spread of install dates and a pile-up of requests at annual windows, which shows up as bursts in the monthly series.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. q_topup, t_pause (F-e only) and F-k (Director's 10% / SG000 reserve) exist, but F-k is only used as an initial source, not as a top-up channel for an overrun. F-f has a single probability and no waiting time or channel choice. The timing and channel selection are missing, so kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.2: Director may adjust the capital budget up to 10% without going back to the Board (RES l.22, l.82); unassigned signal reserve SG000 $1.6M (FY27) + $0.5M (FY28) (CIP27m); CIP rule 'fund urgent needs by stage' (CIPpol p.6); Board wants transfers 'one-time and spread out'. 01 s2.11 and 2.3: SFCTA precedent of a $2.7M top-up for 13th St; a 5YPP revision took 3-4 months (D4 precedent). The ledger gives no wait time for an overrun top-up, so that is no document support.
proposals.parameter: topup_channel with q_topup split by channel and t_wait
proposals.range: channel in {reserve_SG000, director_10pct, annual_CIP, SFCTA_5YPP_amend}; t_wait per channel U(1, 4), U(1, 6), U(6, 12), U(3, 12) months (inferred); channel capacities are shared pools (SG000 about $2.1M total, director cap 10% of the capital budget).
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-f (top-up branch) and F-k; adds a wait state between 'design complete' and 'funded' in the D3.4 local-batch flow.

proposals.behaviour: Delayed disclosure of the overrun. The preparer treats the cost estimate as not final, keeps the design in an open state (for example at a 90% submittal) and does not formally record the overrun until a window opens or a lower-cost scope has been found. Work on the cheap sites continues in the meantime. This is an informal, low-visibility delay tactic and also shields the whole batch from a freeze.
proposals.trigger: Overrun is above contingency but the next funding window is more than a few months away, or the batch is the only live APS line, so a visible overrun could stop it.
proposals.effect_in_model: Inserts a hidden lag t_hide between the overrun being true and the overrun being recognised as a gap. Installs of unaffected sites in the batch go ahead during the lag; the overrun sites do not. The overrun event reaches the event stream and the 25% reporting threshold only after t_hide, so the reported time to overrun differs from the true time. Some of the lag is productive (find a cheaper scope), some is pure delay.
proposals.already_in_model: No. F-f fixes the discovery node to the design-complete date and says 'no separate early investigation'. There is no concealment or hold state.
proposals.evidence: No document support. Nearest line: 01 s2.1 notes the response mode to advocates is cost and lack of funding, which shows framing control but not concealment of an overrun. Treat as a weak, speculative candidate for the sensitivity run only.
proposals.parameter: t_hide
proposals.range: 0 to 12 months, U(0, 6) as the baseline, with a switch sw_hide in {0, 1}; applied only to batches where the overrun exceeds kappa_cont and the next window is more than 3 months away.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-f discovery timing (the 'overrun discovery time point' paragraph) and the event-stream threshold.

proposals.behaviour: Portfolio crowd-out of APS by A2's own higher-value grant applications. The one capital-grants preparer team has a fixed preparation capacity per HSIP/other window and puts it into non-APS packages that score higher or fit the agency's priority categories (SGR, street safety, 'prioritize expansion over maintenance'). The per-agency $10M cap and prep hours are spent elsewhere, so the APS package is never started or is started late and thin.
proposals.trigger: An application window opens while other SFMTA projects compete for the same prep staff and the same per-agency HSIP cap. This is sharpest in hiring-freeze months, and it persists even when advocacy pressure is high.
proposals.effect_in_model: Lowers p_start (or lengthens D_prep) for the APS task in exactly those windows where non-APS work is competing. This makes the 'MISSED' and never-started outcomes depend on the competing workload, not only on strain(t) and pressure.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. R_other (D10) is exogenous and only eats HSIP dollars. strain(t) (D3.2, M-B) lowers p_start for staff shortage in general. Neither says that A2 itself chooses to spend scarce prep capacity on other projects, so the choice is not captured. Not dropped, because the competition for prep time is endogenous and window-specific.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.1: 'one associate engineer scores all applications'; 'policy has no duty to apply for funding'. 01 §2.2: 'grant rules prioritize expansion over maintenance; the most flexible money goes to match' (CIPpol p.11); priority categories have no accessibility item (CIP25 p.4). Direct evidence of A2 choosing other projects over APS: none. The mechanism is inferred.
proposals.parameter: m_crowd: logit penalty on p_start in a window, equal to m_crowd * n_competing(window), where n_competing is the number of non-APS SFMTA packages in preparation in that window (drawn from a rate tied to R_other, or a fixed count).
proposals.range: m_crowd U(0, 2) logit units per competing package; n_competing 0-3. Off = 0 (reproduces the current model).
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 p_start formula (add a term -m_crowd * n_competing), and optionally D_prep in D3.1.

proposals.behaviour: Accounting reclassification to fund APS installs from capital rather than operating money. Signal Shop labor is partly charged to project-support funds (8 of 21 positions). Budget options include 'reorganize work orders so they count as capital' and the CIP is expanding the definition of capital investment. A2 and the finance staff can tag APS retrofits as capital-eligible work, or attach them to an existing capital work order, without any new grant.
proposals.trigger: Pressure from advocates combined with a stated 'no money' line. Also an operating deficit with CIP language that rewards capital-eligible labor.
proposals.effect_in_model: Creates a small unlisted path from the existing Signal Shop crew to Fi installs with no HSIP or Prop L row. It raises effective K_crew funding or adds installs per year at the cost of a lower strain(t) and an extra audit/legitimacy risk. It acts like PW5, but it is triggered by pressure and budget rules, not by a hardware-replacement event.
proposals.already_in_model: Not fully. PW5 (D3.6) funds APS only as an add-on to a button or hardware replacement event, with b_hw as a maintenance quota. The labor-capitalization route and the 'expanded capital definition' are not in 02. Not dropped, because PW5's trigger and funding source differ.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.2: 2025-02 budget options 'move 25% of paint and sign shop staff to capital priorities' and 'reorganize work orders so they count toward capital projects' (sfmta-media-41700 p.9, p.17), not naming Signal Shop; CIP27 plan to 'broaden the capital investment definition' (CIPpol p.10). 01 §2.1: 8/21 electrician positions on project-support funds (38%), 'inference: expected to be recovered by capital projects'. Document support is indirect, because no document names APS.
proposals.parameter: q_capitalize (switch plus probability): per pressure event not deflected, with probability q_capitalize A2 opens a capital-coded work order that funds a_cap dollars per year of APS installs for C-type sites with usable pipes.
proposals.range: q_capitalize U(0, 0.4); a_cap U($0, $150k) per year; sw_capitalize in {0, 1}. Default 0 in the main scenario, run as a sensitivity.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.4 internal delivery (Fi funding source) and D3.1 DEFLECTED branch (adds a third response beside deflect and pressure-stays).

proposals.behaviour: Reporting-metric reframing instead of deflection. When pressed, A2 does not only say 'no money'. It restates progress against a denominator or milestone that has already been met (for example 'eligible' intersections on the high-injury network, 41% vs the 40% target, or 'about one third covered by engineering') so the same pressure counts for less. The pressure event is absorbed, but it is not 'deflected' in the model's sense, and no resource moves.
proposals.trigger: A public or council meeting where advocates cite the 76 unfunded sites, and a ready-made favorable statistic exists. A rise in the number of such statistics after a target has been 'achieved'.
proposals.effect_in_model: Scales down the weight of each pressure event stored in pressure(t), without the r-month DEFLECTED stay in IDLE. Pressure then decays faster or contributes less to p_start. It differs from deflection: the task is not forced into a wait state, but later pressure is also weaker (audience is partly persuaded).
proposals.already_in_model: Only in part. D3.1 has p_deflect, which sends the task to DEFLECTED for r months, and (1 - p_deflect), which lets full pressure into pressure(t). A discount on the pressure that does enter is not modeled. Not dropped, because it changes the pressure stock, not the task state.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.1: the 40% Vision Zero target reported 'achieved' (354/858 = 41%) and no later target; reports of share funded changed from 20 of 71 (2018) to 'most' (2023) to 'about one third' (2026), with the denominator 'about 75'; MDC26 p.3, p.8. Also 01 §2.1 response pattern 'cost and no money' (MDC26 p.4-6). No document says the reframing is deliberate. Model it as a behavior, not an intention.
proposals.parameter: d_reframe: fraction of a non-deflected pressure event's weight removed when A2 reframes, applied with probability q_reframe.
proposals.range: q_reframe U(0, 0.8); d_reframe U(0, 0.7). Off = 0.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 pressure(t) accumulation (Σ exp(-Δt/k) weights) and the branch '1 - p_deflect'.

proposals.behaviour: Delivery-risk aversion: A2 declines to start or enlarge a HSIP package for APS because a late or failed APS project could add a red flag, trigger the 5-year not-in-construction rule, or force a refund of spent preliminary money, and these penalties affect the agency's later higher-value applications. A2 therefore applies only when the package is clearly safe (partner project on schedule, small, internal delivery) and otherwise skips the window.
proposals.trigger: Current red-flag count or recent F-d / F-g events on SFMTA's HSIP portfolio, a partner project (e.g. SG015) running late, or a recently refunded project.
proposals.effect_in_model: Makes p_start for HSIP tasks depend on the agency's own flag history. Fewer submissions after delays, which sustains the spiral of non-applications in a way not tied to advocacy pressure or staff strain.
proposals.already_in_model: No. F-c and F-d (D3.5) and the eligibility check in D3.3 punish red flags, and rho_flag models flags on other projects, but nothing in D3.1's p_start lets A2 anticipate this and avoid applying. Not dropped.
proposals.evidence: 02 D3.3: 'any project not in construction 5 years after selection is ineligible, even if extended'; F-d: red flags affect eligibility of later rounds. 01 §2.4 (Caltrans HSIP) states the delivery requirements (PE 9 months, CON 36 months, refund). No document shows A2 reacting to them. Anticipatory avoidance is an inference.
proposals.parameter: m_flag: logit penalty on p_start for HSIP-route tasks = m_flag * (number of active red flags or F-d/F-g events in the last N months on the agency's portfolio).
proposals.range: m_flag U(0, 1.5) logit per flag; look-back N U(12, 36) months. Off = 0.
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 p_start (HSIP route only), reading state from D3.5 F-c, F-d, F-g.

proposals.behaviour: Descope or substitute within the funded batch. When design shows conduit and curb ramp overruns beyond contingency, the A2 planner drops or defers only the expensive sites and re-spends the freed money on cheaper pool sites. The batch stays funded and installs fewer, cheaper sites, instead of a plain top-up-or-terminate outcome for each site.
proposals.trigger: Design-complete overrun at a site is larger than the remaining contingency, and the top-up request has not yet been won or has failed. Cheaper unfunded C-class sites exist in the pool.
proposals.effect_in_model: A failed top-up no longer only returns the site to the pool. The freed funds can buy cheaper sites, which raises installed counts and lowers the expensive tail. The site that was dropped is parked for another window. This also changes who is served, since the cheap and simple sites go first.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. F-f says that without a top-up the site is TERMINATED and returns to the backlog. D3.4 says terminated funds are released. Nothing says the released money is re-spent on substitute sites in the same batch, so the substitution is not in the model.
proposals.evidence: No document support for substitution itself. Indirect support: 01 §2.1 says 'easy sites are already done, the rest are harder and costlier'. The 2026 MDC statement says remaining sites are 'selected based on funding' (01 §2.1, decision rules).
proposals.parameter: p_swap
proposals.range: 0 to 1; default 0.5. Optionally a lag t_swap of U(1, 4) months
proposals.rule_modified: F-f 'no top-up' branch. With probability p_swap, the freed budget goes back into the same batch's allocation step (cheapest-first within A_local) instead of leaving the system. The sites that were dropped go back to the pool.

proposals.behaviour: Carve out the ramp or conduit portion and shift it to another budget. The planner splits the work into a stripped APS-only scope on the original money and a ramp or excavation scope handed to the Public Works curb-ramp program or a parent paving or utility project. Sites then keep the APS part and the ramp part waits on someone else's budget.
proposals.trigger: Overrun at a site is mostly due to the ramp or conduit add-on, which is the 200k each line in the cost tables. A ramp program or parent project with a live budget covers the same site.
proposals.effect_in_model: The cost that A2 must cover falls to the base APS cost plus any conduit it keeps. The ramp share becomes a dependency on a Public Works delivery clock, which is slow (6 to 9.5 years for contracts). This turns a funding gap into a delay, and it can shift the site into a 'wait for parent' state with its own t_parent.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. D3.4 has 'merge into existing project' with probability pi and parent delay t_parent, but this is a route chosen at the intake stage. Nothing lets the planner move only the overrun component out of an already designed local-batch site. D3.5 F-f has only top-up or terminate.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.11: 'DPW designs ramps with future APS reserved, but ramp construction does not trigger APS; APS is MTA's job'. 01 §2.11 Public Works ramp budget $4.0M to $8.1M. 01 §2.1: 'not touching existing ramps can be five times faster'. 01 §2.2 notes SFMTA budget options to 'reorganise work orders so they count toward capital projects'. The 'five times' and the Public Works handoff are interview claims and untested.
proposals.parameter: q_shift
proposals.range: 0 to 0.5; default 0.2. Companion delay t_shift U(6, 36) months for the ramp part
proposals.rule_modified: F-f. Before a top-up request, with probability q_shift the ramp or conduit share (about 200k or 400k) is removed from the site cost and attached as a dependency on a parent event, as in D3.4 merge-into-project.

proposals.behaviour: Hold the overrun and wait for a better window. A2 does not file the top-up request at once. The planner waits for the next budget cycle or a Prop L / general-fund window, bundles the overrun with a larger request where it looks smaller, or waits until a competing priority has cleared. The site sits in a held state in the meantime.
proposals.trigger: Design-complete overrun happens outside the local preparation window (windows open 1 January and close 30 June, with decisions 1 July), or when the pressure level is low and the board is under an operating deficit.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds a delay to every overrun case and an exposure to repeated misses of the window. The held site stays in the design-complete state and does not enter the crew queue, which lowers installs in the short run. It also lets other shocks (staffing, F-h, F-j) arrive before the request is decided.
proposals.already_in_model: Not for F-f. F-e has t_pause for a second request after a first refusal, and D3.1 has windows for new applications. F-f's top-up is instantaneous with probability q_topup and has no lag or window rule.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.2: capital revenue is short by about 246M, and the board prefers diffused, one-time reallocations. 01 §2.2 notes the annual Jan to July window rhythm for local fields (02 O3 local field dates). No document support for deliberate waiting on overruns specifically.
proposals.parameter: t_topup_wait
proposals.range: U(0, 12) months; or snap to the next local window (0 or about 6 to 12 months)
proposals.rule_modified: F-f. The top-up request becomes a task that must start in a window like PREPARING. The site waits in a HELD state until the next window, then q_topup is drawn.

proposals.behaviour: Reframe the overrun as a safety or ADA scope item to draw a different pot. The planner re-labels the added ramp and conduit cost as an ADA or street-safety capital item, so it can be asked for from the general-fund street-safety share or the director's reallocation rather than from the Prop L APS line.
proposals.trigger: Overrun beyond contingency, and the APS-specific line (EP17 or the local batch) is empty. The ramp content makes the ADA label plausible.
proposals.effect_in_model: Raises the effective q_topup for sites with a large ramp share, and lowers it for conduit-only sites. It makes top-up success depend on cost composition, which the model treats as a single scalar now.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. F-k covers the director's 10 percent and SG000 reserve, with q_dir. The model does not condition the top-up source on what the overrun is made of.
proposals.evidence: 01 §2.6 line 72: a 125M/10-year general-fund ADA right-of-way fund flows to curb ramps, and there is no matching APS fund (inferred). 01 §2.7: MDC support letters in 2025 and 2026 name curb ramps, not APS. 01 §2.2 notes the 25 percent street-safety share of the general fund. No document support that A2 actually relabels.
proposals.parameter: q_topup_ramp
proposals.range: q_topup multiplied by (1 + g * ramp_share), with g in 0 to 1.5
proposals.rule_modified: F-f top-up draw. The probability of top-up depends on the ramp share of the added cost, using the cost split already drawn (200k pipe, 200k ramp).

proposals.behaviour: Offset-funded amendment (zero-sum ask). Because EP17 is over-programmed, staff draft the amendment so the APS line is paid by trimming other SFMTA-owned EP17 lines (e.g. visibility or hardware-replacement lines) rather than asking for new money, so the board is not choosing between APS and controllers on top of the existing overhang.
proposals.trigger: EP17 programmed far above pay-as-you-go and a visible outage-driven controller need exists when the amendment is drafted.
proposals.effect_in_model: Lowers the veto/deferral probability of the amendment (F-j) but shrinks the money available for controller/visibility lines by the same amount, and the APS line size is capped by the offset. Keeps PW2 alive in tight-money years that would otherwise end in veto.
proposals.already_in_model: No. F-j has only an exogenous q_veto and t_defer. PW2 and PW6 fix the ask size and do not let A2 choose how it is financed. D3.6 only has a fallback after veto.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3 (EP17-5YPP p.10-11, p.14): commitment $27.49M vs pay-as-you-go $8.52M (about 202% ahead), FY26-28 money fully assigned, hardware replacement $0.5M/yr and visibility $0.4M/yr. No document support that A2 offsets lines; the offset logic is an inference.
proposals.parameter: offset_frac (default 0): share of the APS line financed by cutting other SFMTA EP17 lines. Effects: q_veto_eff = q_veto*(1 - g*offset_frac), and a_sg017 reduced by offset_frac * APS_line.
proposals.range: offset_frac in [0,1]; g in [0.3,0.8]
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-j and D3.6 PW2 (and a_sg017 in D10)

proposals.behaviour: Outage crowd-out of preparation capacity. After a signal outage, the same staff who would prepare the APS amendment or grant request are pulled to prepare the controller-replacement funding request. APS preparation is paused or lengthened.
proposals.trigger: A citywide or large outage event (the evidence shows two, 2022 and 2025) opens a short window in which the visible failure outranks APS.
proposals.effect_in_model: For a spell after an outage, p_start for APS tasks falls and D_prep for APS rises. It also raises the probability that the SG017 money is used for controllers.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. q_sg017_block (D10) covers SFCTA-side use of SG017 money for failure-priority projects. strain(t) in M-B covers general staffing. No rule makes an outage a shock to A2's own task queue, and no outage event is generated.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3 line 176: result driven by visible failures, controllers received EP17 hardware money after the 2022 and 2025 outages (OCT25 p.7). 01 section 2.1 line 126: about 98 controllers with firewall defects got the $1M. No document support for the preparation-capacity effect itself.
proposals.parameter: outage_crowd switch with lambda_out (outages per year), t_out (duration), x (p_start multiplier p_start*(1-x)) and d_out (extra months added to D_prep).
proposals.range: lambda_out in [0.05,0.4]/yr; t_out in [3,12] months; x in [0,0.8]; d_out in [1,3] months
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 p_start formula and D_prep; D3.2 as a new switch (on in M-B and M-D)

proposals.behaviour: Self-imposed hold for the 5YPP window. Rather than push a standalone amendment into a hostile, over-programmed board, staff quietly hold the request and fold it into the next 5YPP update (2027 fall to 2028), when line items are reset and the over-programming is expected to ease.
proposals.trigger: Pre-submission signals (SFCTA staff, the pay-as-you-go gap) that the amendment will likely fail or be deferred; the 5YPP statement that the next five years will not be ahead to this degree.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds months of delay before PW2 starts and spares the veto draw. The task goes to IDLE until the 5YPP window opens, which moves the timing of the APS money while sometimes raising its eventual chance.
proposals.already_in_model: No. 5YPP appears only as a fallback after the board's veto or deferral (F-j, PW2), a consequence of someone else's decision. A2 never chooses to wait.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3 line 180: 'the next five years are not expected to be ahead to this degree'; 01 section 3.1 line 411: 5YPP revision can go any time (D4 precedent 3-4 months) or wait until 2028; 01 line 190: no EP17 request in the Jan/May/Jun 2026 allocation memos. No document support that A2 deliberately holds.
proposals.parameter: p_hold: when PW2 would start, with probability p_hold the task enters a new WAIT state until the next 5YPP window, then faces q_veto_5ypp instead of q_veto.
proposals.range: p_hold in [0,1] (default 0); q_veto_5ypp in [0.05,0.3]
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 task state machine (new WAIT state) and D3.6 PW2 start

proposals.behaviour: Ask-size shaping: A2 decides how large the amendment request is (a small 'seed' or design-only APS line vs. the full backlog) to fit EP17's thin headroom, instead of a fixed ask whose rejection is an exogenous coin flip.
proposals.trigger: EP17 over-programmed (about 202% ahead of pay-go, near-zero uncommitted headroom of $0-0.5M/yr) and competing controller claims visible to the board.
proposals.effect_in_model: Rejection/deferral chance rises with the ask relative to headroom. A smaller ask lowers veto but delivers fewer intersections per year and pushes later tranches to the next 5YPP round, so the path may be 'cheaper to approve, slower to cover'.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. F-j has q_veto U(0,0.5) and t_defer (02 D3.5), but q_veto is a constant independent of ask size. PW2 has no ask-size choice. The size choice itself is not modelled, so kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 2.3: 'FY26-28 unallocated headroom $0-0.5M/yr' (EP17-5YPP p.14); 5YPP committed $27.49M vs pay-go $8.52M (about 202%); SP cut projects to 85-89% of priority 1. No document that A2 sizes its ask; the ask-size choice itself has no document support.
proposals.parameter: ask_frac (share of the full APS need requested in the amendment); q_veto = q0 + k_ask*max(0, ask/headroom - 1)
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-j and the PW2 starting move; D10 q_veto becomes a function instead of a constant.

proposals.behaviour: Piggyback timing on a failure event: A2 files or re-files the amendment in the window right after a controller outage or a visible failure, when the board is already in 'fix visible failure' mode, and frames APS-ready controllers as part of resilience.
proposals.trigger: A controller outage or other visible signal failure (2022 and 2025 outages each produced EP17 hardware money). Inside the window, bundling with the controller claim can lower the veto chance. The cost is that APS ends up competing inside the same pot.
proposals.effect_in_model: Within a window of w months after an outage shock, q_veto is multiplied by (1 - g) if A2 piggybacks, but the amendment's APS share is capped by what is left after the controller claim (a_pig). Outside the window A2 waits (a delay, not a filing).
proposals.already_in_model: No. PW6 (D3.6) only lists 'money used up by controller priority' as a blocking cause (q_sg017_block); outage is not an event that A2 uses to time or reframe a request, and F-j has no outage-linked window. Kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 2.3 line 176: 'results are visible-failure driven: controllers got EP17 hardware money after the 2022 and 2025 outages'; 01 2.1 line 126: $1M FY25+FY26 went to about 98 controllers although the 2023 PIF listed APS replacement as eligible. No document support that A2 deliberately times filings to outages.
proposals.parameter: sw_piggyback (0/1), g, w, a_pig
proposals.range: sw_piggyback in {0,1}; g U(0, 0.5); w U(1, 6) months; a_pig U(0, 0.5) of the line
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-j (q_veto) and the O3 event table (outage shock added); D3.6 PW2 filing time.

proposals.behaviour: Reprogramming instead of new money: A2 requests a zero-net amendment that takes money from other EP17 sub-lines (visibility, TSP, signs) rather than adding APS above the line, which avoids a contest with controller replacements but needs another sponsor's consent. A second variant is to wait for the 2027-28 5YPP round, when a new APS line can be scored on equal terms.
proposals.trigger: The over-programmed state means any new line must displace an existing one, and the 'next 5YPP will not be this far ahead' statement means the pot gets thinner.
proposals.effect_in_model: Amendment cost switches from 'new dollars' to 'a conflict with other line holders'. With probability q_swap the board treats it as zero-net and approves faster; but the donor line's output (delivery rate in the model) is cut, and the APS share is limited to what the donor lines can give (a_swap).
proposals.already_in_model: No. PW6/F-j treat the amendment only as an approve/deny of added money; no rule moves money between EP17 lines or waits for the 5YPP round except as a fallback after a veto (D3.6 PW2 'wait for next 5YPP' is only a fallback after a veto, not a chosen tactic). Kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 2.3 lines 179-180: FY26-28 about $2.80M/yr all given to TSP, pipes, signs, hardware replacement ($0.5M/yr), visibility ($0.4M/yr); 'next five years not expected to be this far ahead'. No document that anyone has proposed a swap; no document support for the tactic itself.
proposals.parameter: sw_swap (0/1, tactic chosen) with q_swap and a_swap
proposals.range: q_swap U(0.2, 0.8); a_swap U($0, $400k)/yr (bounded by the visibility + hardware lines, $0.9M/yr); sw_swap in {0,1,2} where 2 = wait for next 5YPP round
proposals.rule_modified: D3.5 F-j and D3.6 PW2 (start step); D10 adds three parameters.

proposals.behaviour: Ring-fencing by drafting. When writing the SG017 allocation request, the preparer names APS as an explicit line item or sub-scope with a dollar figure, or leaves it as a generic 'hardware replacement' that controller needs can absorb. The wording choice changes how likely the money is later used for controllers instead of APS.
proposals.trigger: The CIP scope text already allows new APS, but the last two allocations (FY24, FY25-26) went to cabinets/detectors/RRFB and about 98 controllers. A request drafted the same way again will be read the same way.
proposals.effect_in_model: Turns q_sg017_block from a purely exogenous draw into one that the PW6 request can lower (named APS sub-line) or raise (generic wording). It also fixes a_sg017 as a stated amount in the request rather than a leftover.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. D10 has q_sg017_block (U(0.2,0.9)) and a_sg017 (U(0,250k)), and PW6 says 'write new APS into the SG017 request' (02 D3.6 PW6, line 245). But both are exogenous probabilities; the model has no switch for how the A2 drafts the request. Not a full duplicate, so kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 3.2 (line ~446): CIP27m scope text includes new APS 'where conduits and poles are satisfactory', while the 5YPP description says only 'replace'. 01 section 2.1: EP17 $1M went to controllers although the 2023 PIF listed APS replacement as an eligible use. No document shows how SFMTA words its requests, so the mechanism itself has no document support.
proposals.parameter: w_earmark: share of the SG017 request written as an explicit APS line, 0 to 0.5. Applied as q_sg017_block_eff = q_sg017_block * (1 - k_earmark * w_earmark/0.5), with k_earmark U(0, 0.6) (inference). Also reduces a_sg017 variance, since it sets the amount.
proposals.range: w_earmark in {0, 0.25, 0.5}; k_earmark U(0, 0.6)
proposals.rule_modified: D3.2 PW6 trigger and q_sg017_block (D10)

proposals.behaviour: Co-bundling APS onto the controller replacement itself. The preparer frames APS install as part of the cabinet/controller job at the same intersection, so the one visit and one request cover both. This turns controller demand from a competitor for the money into a carrier for it.
proposals.trigger: The controller replacement list (about 98 sites in the last round) is the real funded work. The cabinet is already open and the sites are already scheduled. The staff view is that 'installing with existing work is cheapest'.
proposals.effect_in_model: A subset of C-type intersections on a controller-replacement list get APS at lower unit cost and with no separate SG017 competition. The alternative PW6 failure (money consumed by controllers) becomes a delivery path instead.
proposals.already_in_model: No. 02 treats bundling only for HSIP (D3.3, SI02/SI07 carriers, F-g partner projects). Controllers appear only as the blocker q_sg017_block. Co-bundling with controllers inside SG017 is not a rule.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.1: 'All new signals and major upgrades get APS; installing alongside existing work is cheapest' (MDC23 p.6; MDC26 p.7). 01 section 3.2: the FY25-26 controller job covered about 98 intersections. Whether APS poles/conduit/PCS are adequate at those sites is unknown, so this has no direct document support for APS.
proposals.parameter: f_cobundle: fraction of the A2's SG017 request treated as controller+APS joint scope, 0 to 0.4, applied to the 'poles and conduit adequate' share of C-type sites (p_adequate, existing 0.42-0.72 range). Cost multiplier on those sites c_joint U(0.5, 0.9) of the stand-alone unit cost (inference).
proposals.range: f_cobundle 0 to 0.4; c_joint U(0.5, 0.9); gated by p_adequate
proposals.rule_modified: D3.4 delivery and PW6 allocation split (new split inside a_sg017)

proposals.behaviour: Waiting for the HSIP result before committing SG017 to APS. The preparer holds the APS share out of the SG017 request until Cycle 13 is decided, to avoid spending local money that HSIP might fund, or to avoid being told later that APS was the weaker request.
proposals.trigger: CIP lists SG142 APS FY27 as HSIP Cycle 13 (2027) EST money alongside SG017. A request prepared before the HSIP decision risks double-funding the same sites.
proposals.effect_in_model: A time lag t_wait_hsip before PW6 can start APS spending. If HSIP fails (F-a/F-b), the local share is released and PW6 starts late. If HSIP succeeds, SG017 goes to controllers and PW6 contributes nothing.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. D3.1 has windows and PREPARING time, and D3.6 has adaptive pathways with fallback from HSIP to local money. But there is no deliberate 'hold the local request until the other source resolves' rule; the sequence is fixed by the path, not chosen by the A2.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.1: SG015 and SG142 are listed separately in the CIP with the same HSIP source and the same FY28 column. No document shows SFMTA holding SG017 back in this way; no document support for the behaviour.
proposals.parameter: sw_wait: boolean, with delay t_wait_hsip U(0, 18) months applied to PW6 start only when an HSIP application is pending.
proposals.range: sw_wait in {0,1}; t_wait_hsip U(0, 18) months
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 IDLE->PREPARING start condition for SG017 requests, and PW6 sequencing

proposals.behaviour: Scope drift after allocation. Once SG017 money is granted with a broad 'hardware' scope, SFMTA reassigns it to controllers or other failing equipment as emergencies appear (cyber vulnerabilities, 220 deferred maintenance sites), with the APS share shrinking without any new request.
proposals.trigger: A fault or vulnerability list with a deadline appears after allocation, and the staff member sees that using the money on APS leaves no reserve for it.
proposals.effect_in_model: a_sg017 shrinks over the grant period. Sites can drop out after APPROVED status, which currently happens only via PIF, cost overrun or partner failures (F-d to F-g).
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. q_sg017_block covers 'money used up by controllers and other fault priorities' at the allocation step (D10 line 375, PW6). It does not cover drift after the allocation is made, and F-f only covers cost increases.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.1: the 'EP17 $1M to about 98 controllers' row and the line 'in 2024-09, maintenance and preventive work at 220 priority intersections was deferred' (staffing media 41356 p.19, p.22). Drift after allocation itself is an inference.
proposals.parameter: lambda_drift: annual rate at which the not-yet-installed APS share of an SG017 grant is reassigned, 0 to 0.4 per year, with a share d_drift U(0.3, 1) of the remaining APS amount moved per event.
proposals.range: lambda_drift U(0, 0.4)/yr; d_drift U(0.3, 1)
proposals.rule_modified: D3.4 delivery (new failure path F-n next to F-f/F-g) and a_sg017 after APPROVED

proposals.behaviour: Dated-promise placation. At the council meeting SFMTA staff answer pressure with a soft commitment ("we will install as signal work and funding allow", or a promised report-back) instead of only "costly, no money". The promise discharges pressure for a while, starts no task, and if nothing follows, credibility erodes and the next round of pressure comes back stronger.
proposals.trigger: A pressure event at a public body (disability council) where the cost/no-money answer alone would be re-challenged, and A2 holds no funded vehicle to point at.
proposals.effect_in_model: A third response branch next to DEFLECTED and 'pressure stays'. Pressure is set to near zero for t_promise months with no task start. If no application instance has been SUBMITTED by the end of the window, pressure returns at a multiple (1+rebound) of its prior level. This gives a calm-then-spike pattern in pressure(t) and a longer idle time before the first PREPARING.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly, and the overlap is only with the cost/no-money answer. D3.1 DEFLECTED (p_deflect, r months) leaves no lasting effect, and F-m covers advocacy going quiet. Neither has a promise that sets a later credibility penalty, so the rebound term is new. Not dropped.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.7.1 row 2009-11-20: the planning-department staff reply was that MTA would install 'with signal improvements, or by public-request score', 'no date, no funding'. Inference at the end of 2.7.1: that 2009 sentence is the prototype of today's two channels, with no time or money attached. Same section, row 2026-09-18: the ODA promise to come back with recommendations shows no follow-up in the public agenda. This supports promises made without delivery but not the rebound term (no document support for the rebound).
proposals.parameter: p_placate (share of pressure events answered by a no-money promise) U(0, 0.5); t_promise U(3, 12) months; rebound U(0, 1) multiplier on pressure when the promise lapses unfulfilled.
proposals.range: p_placate U(0,0.5); t_promise U(3,12) months; rebound U(0,1)
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 pressure-event rule. Branch probabilities become p_deflect, p_placate, and 1 - p_deflect - p_placate. During t_promise, pressure(t) is zeroed in the p_start logistic. At lapse with no SUBMITTED instance, pressure(t) is multiplied by (1+rebound).

proposals.behaviour: Anticipatory abstention because of open red flags. A2 skips or postpones an APS package for a cycle when the agency already carries an HSIP project with an open delivery red flag, or when the APS package depends on a risky partner project. A2 does this to avoid a rejection at eligibility review and to protect SFMTA's standing for its higher-value HSIP projects.
proposals.trigger: An existing red flag (PE over 9 months, CON over 36/42 months) on any SFMTA HSIP project, or a known delay on the partner project (F-g), at the time of the prep decision before the deadline.
proposals.effect_in_model: Lowers p_start in HSIP windows only, before the work starts. Fewer MISSED and REJECTED outcomes and more silent IDLE, so the failure mode moves from 'rejected' (F-c) to 'never tried'. The list state shows no trace, as the model itself says for unfiled applications.
proposals.already_in_model: Not in the logistic. D3.1 says preparation and submission are not blocked early because of eligibility, and 'submission does not check red flags'. F-c models rejection only after review. The model never lets A2 foresee the flag. Not a duplicate of F-h or F-i, which act on capacity, not on expected rejection.
proposals.evidence: no document support in 01 for A2 anticipation. The only support is the rule in 02 D3.5 F-d that red flags affect eligibility in later rounds. Treat this as an inferred behaviour.
proposals.parameter: beta_flag, U(0, 2): a new term -beta_flag * 1[open_flag or partner_delay > theta] in p_start, HSIP window only.
proposals.range: beta_flag U(0,2)
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 p_start logistic formula. Can be switched off in M-A and M-B to keep the mechanisms separable.

proposals.behaviour: Status-label drift. When asked why 76 are unfunded, staff move intersections on the request list to 'funded with a signal project' (Fs) or 'in design' on a loose reading of a parent project, without a confirmed parent or install order. The pending count shrinks and pressure falls. The real work stays unfunded until later reconciliation.
proposals.trigger: Public attention to the size of the list. Also any large upcoming signal or corridor project that could be said to cover nearby intersections.
proposals.effect_in_model: Stochastic C/N to Fs reclassification not tied to a funded vehicle. The visible pending stock drops; the true uninstalled stock does not. Those Fs then enter the Fs to I hazard (h_fs) and show up as delayed or stuck. This is a source of observed Fs counts without real tasks.
proposals.already_in_model: Not as an actor choice. The 'done3' parameter (D10) treats stale records as a data question (real undelivered vs lagging record, equal probability), and the 5 unidentified-parent Fs are modelled as route 'unidentified parent'. Neither lets A2 produce the drift as a response to pressure. Not dropped, but keep it separate from done3.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 3.2 (line ~467): the official Fs status says 'with a funded signal project' while the parent is complete, a contradiction between a handover not done or a lagging list. Line ~481: 5 Fs have no identifiable parent in the public CIP or project pages. The evidence shows the labels exist; it does not show intent, so the behaviour is an inference.
proposals.parameter: r_label: monthly rate at which a C or N intersection is relabelled Fs without a funded parent, active only if pressure(t) > theta_p.
proposals.range: r_label U(0, 0.02) per month
proposals.rule_modified: O2 state transitions of the list (C/N to Fs) and the pressure input; F4 calibration (Fs stock 19-23) must separate real Fs from relabelled Fs. Off in the base run, report as sensitivity only.

proposals.behaviour: Strategic waiting for a better window. A2 deliberately does not start HSIP preparation in the nearer cycle because it expects local (Prop L) money in the next 5-year program to be easier, faster and less encumbered than federal money, and says publicly that APS 'is in the next programming cycle'.
proposals.trigger: A local window opens within H months of an HSIP deadline, with non-zero uncommitted local margin, while federal conditions (BCR 5.0, PIF, outsourcing) look worse than local ones.
proposals.effect_in_model: HSIP prep decisions depend on what other windows will offer. A2 skips the HSIP deadline and holds the task in IDLE until the local window, even when the HSIP package would have passed. This shifts first-funding time by one cycle and changes which pathways (PW1 vs PW2) the signposts see.
proposals.already_in_model: Only forced waiting: F-j (Prop L amendment vetoed, then wait for the next 5YPP) and D3.6 'turn to the next usable window' after a failure. There is no voluntary skip made before trying. Not dropped.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3 (Prop L EP17 5YPP 2027 autumn to 2028; FY26-28 uncommitted margin $0-0.5M per year) and 02 O2 window list give the timing. Nothing in 01 records A2 choosing to wait: no document support for the choice itself.
proposals.parameter: beta_wait, subtracted in p_start as -beta_wait * 1[other window opens within H months and A_local_expected > 0]; H in months.
proposals.range: beta_wait U(0,2); H U(6,18) months
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 p_start formula (HSIP window only). Compare under M-C (cost pressure), where the rule is most likely to act.

proposals.behaviour: Match-fund reframing. The staff member pitches the APS line as local match that unlocks federal and state money (HSIP 10%, SS4A 20% match), not as a standalone safety spend. A small dedicated Prop L line is justified by the multiple of outside dollars it draws.
proposals.trigger: EP17 is over-programmed and controller replacements are competing. The staff member needs a reason that beats a visible outage fix. The 5YPP scoring has a leverage criterion.
proposals.effect_in_model: Raises board approval odds for the amendment when leverage is high, and couples the line to HSIP/SS4A packaging (PW1): each Prop L dollar carries 1/match_rate federal dollars. Cost: the money is conditional, so if the federal bid fails the line sits idle (new failure branch).
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. PW2 (02 D3.6) treats Prop L and HSIP as sequential fallbacks, not one linked ask. D10 has match rates only as an HSIP eligibility cost. No rule makes amendment approval depend on federal leverage, so kept.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.3 l.186: 5YPP scoring includes leverage (4 points). 01 s2.2 l.149: 'the most flexible money must go to match'. 01 s2.5 l.240: Tenderloin SS4A, $1.4M Prop L against $5.6M federal. 01 s5 l.604-606: match rates 10% / 20%.
proposals.parameter: match_framing in {0,1} with gamma_lev U(0, 0.15): p_approve = base + gamma_lev * leverage_weight * (1/match_rate)/10; when 1, line release is conditional on an HSIP/SS4A award.
proposals.range: match_framing {0,1}; gamma_lev U(0, 0.15); leverage_weight U(0,1)
proposals.rule_modified: PW2 first-step amendment approval (02 D3.6) and the A_local release rule (D10 line 358)

proposals.behaviour: Sizing the ask to the headroom or funding it by an offset inside EP17. With unprogrammed margin of only $0-0.5M/yr, the staff member asks for a token line, or proposes taking the money from another EP17 line (hardware replacement, visibility) so the amendment looks total-neutral.
proposals.trigger: The amendment would add to a plan about 202% ahead of cash. The staff member knows the real room before drafting.
proposals.effect_in_model: Replaces the free draw A_local U(0.5M, 2M) with a request bounded by headroom H plus an offset share. Offsets cut the hardware/controller line and raise q_sg017_block. Smaller asks are approved more often but cap installed volume.
proposals.already_in_model: No. D10 line 358 draws A_local U(0.5M,2M) without checking it against the $0-0.5M/yr headroom (D10 line 613), and q_sg017_block (line 375) is exogenous, not responsive to offsets.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.3 l.179: EP17 FY24-28 commits $27.49M vs $8.52M pay-go (about 202% ahead), no APS line. 01 s5 l.613: headroom $0 to ~$0.5M/yr; 'only change the hardware replacement line or amend the 5YPP'. 01 s2.3 l.176: controllers got EP17 hardware money after two outages.
proposals.parameter: x_offset: request R = min(R_desired, H + x_offset*R_desired); q_sg017_block' = q_sg017_block + k_off * x_offset * R.
proposals.range: x_offset U(0,1); k_off U(0,0.5); H U($0,$0.5M)/yr
proposals.rule_modified: A_local draw under dedicated_line = 1 (D10 line 358) and q_sg017_block coupling (D10 line 375)

proposals.behaviour: Strategic waiting for the plan window. Rather than file a mid-cycle amendment while controller needs are acute, the staff member holds the request and rolls it into the 2027-fall 5YPP update, so it is one scored item, not a standalone exception.
proposals.trigger: A recent outage or pending controller allocation makes APS look discretionary; the 5YPP window is a known number of months away.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds an applicant-chosen delay D_wait before PW2 starts, in exchange for an approval bonus. Lengthens the idle period (recovery_time) and delays the Prop L branch's fallback to general fund / HSIP.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. theta_defer (D10 line 384) covers board-caused delay only. PW2 in D3.6 has only the immediate amendment, though the evidence lists both options. Kept as applicant-side choice.
proposals.evidence: 01 s3.1 l.411: 'a 5YPP amendment can go any time (D4 precedent 3-4 months), or wait for 2028'. 01 s2.3 l.177: the Lincoln Way amendment took 3-4 months after a visible trigger.
proposals.parameter: p_wait (chance the applicant defers to the window) and delta_window (approval bonus when filed at the window).
proposals.range: p_wait U(0,0.6); delta_window U(0,0.2); D_wait set by calendar to 2027-10
proposals.rule_modified: PW2 start timing and the theta_defer branch (02 D3.6, D10 line 384)

proposals.behaviour: Pre-briefing advocates and the advisory committee so the amendment arrives with visible support against the outage-driven controller need.
proposals.trigger: A competing need on the same agenda; the staff member knows scoring rewards community support and benefit to disadvantaged groups.
proposals.effect_in_model: Raises amendment approval odds and diverts part of the advocacy pressure(t) from pushing on A2 into support for this specific item.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly. Advocates only generate pressure events and litigation tiers (D1, lambda_press). No rule has A2 recruiting them as supporters or the board scoring responding to it.
proposals.evidence: 01 s2.3 l.186: 5YPP scoring gives community support 5 and disadvantaged populations 5. 01 s2.3 l.188: the advisory committee has advice power only, and its recommendations have matched board action.
proposals.parameter: prebrief in {0,1}: adds delta_support to p_approve and removes pressure_diversion of pressure(t) in that window.
proposals.range: prebrief {0,1}; delta_support U(0,0.15); pressure_diversion U(0,0.5)
proposals.rule_modified: PW2 amendment approval draw and pressure(t) update

proposals.behaviour: Budget-neutral offset offer. Because EP17 is over-programmed, A2 drafts the amendment as a swap: APS money is taken from a named donor line in the same 5-year plan (e.g. deferring part of a hardware-replacement or visibility line) rather than asking for new money, before the board hearing.
proposals.trigger: Amendment being prepared while EP17 uncommitted margin is about zero; also on resubmission after a first deferral or veto (F-j).
proposals.effect_in_model: Lowers veto/deferral probability of the amendment only if a donor line exists. Cost: the donor (hardware/controller) line loses money, so a successful swap raises later `q_sg017_block`. Net APS amount stays small (about $0.25-0.5M/yr).
proposals.already_in_model: No. F-j (02 D3.5) has a single exogenous `q_veto` and `t_defer`. PW2 (02 D3.6) says only 'EP17 amendment restores APS line', with no donor line or trade-off. PW6 covers writing APS into an SG017 request, a different mechanism.
proposals.evidence: 01 section 2.3 line 179: EP17 promises $27.49M vs pay-go $8.52M (about 202% ahead); FY26-28 about $2.80M/yr fully assigned; no APS line. 01 line 613: uncommitted margin $0-0.5M/yr. 01 lines 126/176: controllers got EP17 hardware money after the 2022 and 2025 outages. No document directly shows an offset offer; the behaviour is inference.
proposals.parameter: `sw_offset` (0/1); `q_veto_offset` U(0.05, 0.4) replaces `q_veto` when on; `delta_donor` U(0.5, 1.0) = share of APS amount taken from the SG017 line, which raises `q_sg017_block` proportionally.
proposals.range: sw_offset in {0,1}; q_veto_offset 0.05-0.4; delta_donor 0.5-1.0
proposals.rule_modified: F-j veto/defer probability (D3.5); PW2 start and PW6 `q_sg017_block` (D3.6).

proposals.behaviour: Ask-size shrinking. A2 sizes the amendment to the visible margin (token $0.25-0.5M/yr line rather than full backlog cost) so the board sees an easy yes.
proposals.trigger: Over-programmed plan with about $0-0.5M/yr margin; SFCTA staff signal large asks go to the next 5YPP window (2027 autumn-2028).
proposals.effect_in_model: Approval probability up, sites funded per year down. The 76-site backlog clears slowly and rising unit cost ($20k to $40k, 9-10%/yr) eats the small line. Also changes Signal Shop load.
proposals.already_in_model: No. No ask-size variable exists on the Prop L route; F-j is binary and amount is fixed by the plan. Only the HSIP route has sizing (D3.3 packing), and that is BCR-driven not margin-driven.
proposals.evidence: 01 line 613: uncommitted margin $0 to about $0.5M/yr. 01 section 2.1: unit cost floor $20k (2018) to $40k (2026). 01 line 180: 'next five years not expected to be this far ahead'. No document shows A2 deliberately shrinking an ask (inference).
proposals.parameter: `ask_scale` U(0.25, 1.0); `p_pass = p_pass_full + gamma_ask*(1 - ask_scale)` with `gamma_ask` U(0, 0.4); funded sites/yr = ask_scale x baseline.
proposals.range: ask_scale 0.25-1.0; gamma_ask 0-0.4
proposals.rule_modified: PW2 start step and F-j veto probability (D3.5/D3.6); local-batch size rule (D3.4).

proposals.behaviour: Relabel APS inside an already-programmed EP17 line other than SG017 (visibility, signal upgrade lines) so no amendment is needed and the item does not compete as a new line against controller replacement.
proposals.trigger: Amendment judged likely to fail or be deferred (perceived `q_veto` high), or a recent outage has made controller replacement the visible priority.
proposals.effect_in_model: Adds a route that skips the board amendment (no F-j), but money comes from a line already full, so it is capped by that line's margin and exposed to outage-driven reallocation. Success depends on SFCTA accepting the scope reading at allocation.
proposals.already_in_model: Partly: PW6 (02 D3.6) uses the SG017 CIP text allowing new APS. It does not cover other lines (visibility, TSP, conduit). Only the other-line relabel is proposed.
proposals.evidence: 01 line 179: FY26-28 EP17 money goes to TSP, conduit, signs, hardware replacement ($0.5M/yr), visibility ($0.4M/yr); no APS line. 01 line 126: 2023 PIF listed APS replacement as eligible, yet $1M went to about 98 controllers. No document shows relabelling of the visibility line; inference.
proposals.parameter: `sw_relabel` (0/1); `q_relabel_ok` U(0.1, 0.6) = chance SFCTA accepts scope at allocation; `r_line_share` U(0.1, 0.5) = share of host line available to APS.
proposals.range: sw_relabel in {0,1}; q_relabel_ok 0.1-0.6; r_line_share 0.1-0.5
proposals.rule_modified: Adds an alternative first step in PW2/PW6 before the F-j check (D3.6); amount capped by host line margin and subject to `q_sg017_block`-type crowding.

proposals.behaviour: Outage-timed submission (waiting for a better window). A2 holds the amendment until a visible system failure, since failures drive funding, then files APS as a companion to the controller item, or after controller money is secured so the two do not compete in the same hearing.
proposals.trigger: Outage event (2022, 2025 type) or approaching 5YPP update window; stand-alone ask looks weak in an over-programmed plan.
proposals.effect_in_model: Start time of the amendment tied to an outage signal, not the monthly `p_start` draw. Shifts PW2 later but may raise approval when attached to the failure; splits controller and APS asks into two hearings.
proposals.already_in_model: No. 01 line 176 notes failure-driven funding, but 02 D3.1 `p_start` has terms only for owner, specified, oversight, pressure, enforce, strain and costpress; no outage term and no deliberate wait.
proposals.evidence: 01 line 176: 'result is failure-driven: controllers got EP17 hardware money after 2022 and 2025 outages' (labelled inference). 01 line 190: no EP17 signal request in Jan/May/Jun 2026 SFCTA grant memos. No document of waiting tactics by A2.
proposals.parameter: `sw_wait_outage` (0/1); outage rate `lambda_outage` U(0.1, 0.5)/yr; when on, amendment start requires an outage in the last `w_out` months (U(3, 12)), and `beta_out` U(0, 1.5) is added to the approval logit.
proposals.range: lambda_outage 0.1-0.5/yr; w_out 3-12 months; beta_out 0-1.5
proposals.rule_modified: D3.1 `p_start` (outage term and trigger condition for the PW2 amendment task); F-j approval probability.

proposals.behaviour: Outage-driven reserve hoarding: after a visible signal failure event (citywide power outage, controller security flaw) the SFMTA application writer pulls the whole SG017 ask back to controller and cabinet work and drops or defers the APS line, as a self-imposed risk reserve, before SFCTA ever sees the request.
proposals.trigger: A stochastic failure shock (outage or controller-vulnerability event) in the 12 months before the SG017 request is drafted.
